abstract: Diverse and globally representative datasets are essential to genomic science and medicine. Here, we analyzed population descriptor metadata from RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) studies in two major public repositories: the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) and the Database of Genotypes and Phenotypes. We examined geographic and economic characteristics of institutions depositing the data and compared SRA-deposited descriptors to empirical estimates of genetic ancestry and to those reported in publications, analyzing trends over time. We found that 55% of RNA-seq samples were deposited by United States (US) institutions and 90% by institutions in high-income countries. Only 3% of SRA samples were associated with population descriptors, and among those with US Census terms, 69% were labeled as White. Among samples with continental descriptors, 56% were labeled as European. Our analyses emphasize widespread bias in the composition of public RNA-seq datasets and, more generally, a lack of consistent and careful reporting of population descriptors needing urgent improvement.
